Semantic-aware Token Selection and Resource Optimization for Communication-efficient Split Federated Fine-tuning in Edge Intelligence

Xianke Qiang    Zheng Chang    Geyong Min ††thanks: X. Qiang and Z. Chang are with School of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu 611731, China. G. Min is with Department of Computer Science, University of Exeter, Exeter, EX4 4QF, U.K.
Abstract

Deploying large Transformer-based vision models on resource-limited mobile devices at network edge is severely constrained by hardware limitations and dynamic wireless environments. While federated learning (FL) enables collaborative training without sharing raw data, strictly local fine-tuning of such massive models remains computationally prohibitive for edge devices. Split federated learning (SFL) alleviates this burden by offloading deep layers to the edge server, yet it suffers from heavy communication overhead when transmitting high-dimensional activation tokens. To address this bottleneck, we propose ST-SFLora, a semantic token-based split federated LoRA fine-tuning framework. We introduce a new metric, Semantic Transmission Efficiency (STE), to balance semantic retention and transmission cost. Based on STE, we formulate a joint resource optimization problem that dynamically determines token selection, uplink bandwidth allocation, and transmit power under latency and energy constraints. The resulting mixed-integer nonconvex problem is efficiently solved via an alternating algorithm. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that ST-SFLora achieves the lowest client-side resource consumption among baselines while delivering a favorable trade-off between communication efficiency and model performance.

Index Terms: 
split federated learning, resource allocation, vision transformer, fine-tuning, token selection.

I Introduction

Driven by rapid advances in Aritifical Intelligence (AI), Transformer-based foundation models such as BERT [1], ViT [2], and GPT [3] have achieved state-of-the-art performance in natural language processing and computer vision, demonstrating strong scalability and generalization across modalities. Their success is largely enabled by the pre-training and fine-tuning paradigm, which allows large models to be adapted efficiently to downstream tasks[4]. At the same time, the rapid proliferation of intelligent devices in mobile edge computing (MEC) systems is generating large volumes of decentralized and privacy-sensitive data at the wireless edge [5]. Relying on cloud-based centralized learning to collect raw data from edge devices raises critical concerns, including privacy exposure and excessive bandwidth consumption [6]. Federated learning (FL)[7, 8] addresses these issues by keeping data local and aggregating model updates on the server. However, fine-tuning Transformer-based large models on heterogeneous edge devices remains highly challenging. Even with parameter-efficient techniques such as LoRA, the memory footprint and communication demand of these models still exceed the capabilities of typical mobile devices[9].

To overcome the limitations of on-device fine-tuning, Split Learning (SL)[10] and Split Federated Learning (SFL)[11] offload most computation from clients to the server by partitioning the model between the two sides. However, when applied to large Transformer architectures, these approaches introduce new communication bottlenecks. Traditional SFL requires transmitting client-side weights, intermediate activations, and activation gradients in every iteration[11, 12]. Among these, uploading high-dimensional activations dominates the communication cost[13]. For example, the activations produced by a ViT-B/16 model for a single batch can exceed tens of megabytes1, which is particularly problematic in mobile scenarios where bandwidth fluctuates with channel conditions and connectivity is frequently intermittent. To reduce this communication overhead, existing approaches typically rely on bit-level compression techniques such as quantization [14, 13] and sparsification[15].

11footnotetext: Calculated based on a batch size of 64, a sequence length of 197 (14×\times14 patches plus one class token), and a hidden dimension of 768 with 32-bit floating-point precision. The total size is 64×197×768×464\times 197\times 768\times 4 bytes ≈\approx 37 MB.

As wireless networks advance toward 6G, communication paradigms are shifting from bit-level transmission to task-oriented semantic transmission, where only information relevant to task performance is conveyed and redundant content is suppressed[16]. This evolution aligns naturally with attention mechanism of Transformer-based SL/SFL, in which activations are inherently represented as sequences of semantic tokens rather than raw bits. As shown schematically in Fig. 1, the attention maps can highlight task-relevant patches and ignore background regions, so that only the most informative tokens need to be sent over the 6G link. These tokens contribute unequally to the final prediction [17]. This leads to a natural question: can we compress activations at the semantic token level rather than at the bit level?

Although semantic-aware token-level compression holds promise, applying it to large-scale SFL in MEC environments presents three fundamental challenges:

  • •

    Unlike FL, which exchanges gradients or parameter updates at the bit level, SL/SFL transmits intermediate activations that, in Transformer models, are naturally tokenized and semantically structured. This enables semantic cues to be extracted at the token level rather than treating activations as raw bitstreams. The challenge is to design an SFL architecture that exposes these semantic cues directly from the backbone while keeping clients lightweight and avoiding additional semantic encoders, scoring networks, or auxiliary modules.

  • •

    Since not all tokens contribute equally to the downstream task, transmitting full activation sequences is inefficient. The challenge is to design a principled selection mechanism that leverages the backbone’s attention scores to identify and retain task-relevant tokens, while remaining robust under heterogeneous data distributions and mobile conditions.

  • •

    Token selection introduces a trade-off between semantic information retention and communication overhead. The challenge is to formulate a semantic-aware metric and an optimization problem that balance this trade-off by jointly determining the number of transmitted tokens and the uplink bandwidth and transmit power allocation, under latency and energy constraints.

To tackle these challenges, we propose ST-SFLora, a semantic token-based split federated LoRA fine-tuning framework with three key designs. First, we adopt a one-way uplink SFL architecture in which clients only run lightweight forward passes and upload selected token activations, while avoiding gradient feedback and any extra semantic/scoring modules on devices; this keeps the client logic simple, improves scalability, and enables elastic participation under unreliable mobile connectivity. Second, we exploit the Transformer’s native attention signals to build a semantic-aware token selection strategy, reusing attention weights to identify the most informative tokens without modifying the backbone or introducing noticeable computational overhead. Finally, we introduce a system-level metric, Semantic Transmission Efficiency (STE), to quantify the trade-off between semantic preservation and communication cost under token compression, and use it to couple token selection with bandwidth and power allocation for unified communication resource optimization in ST-SFLora.

To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first attempt to integrate semantic-aware token selection with split federated LoRA fine-tuning for edge intelligence. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose ST-SFLora, a decoupled training framework where clients perform only lightweight forward propagation to extract activation tokens, while all trainable LoRA parameters reside on the server. A key design is to select task-relevant tokens before uplink transmission to balance semantic retention and communication cost, leading to a smaller activation payload in mobile scenarios.

  • •

    We define a novel metric, Semantic Transmission Efficiency (STE), to fundamentally quantify the system-level trade-off between semantic information retention and communication latency. Unlike traditional throughput metrics, STE explicitly characterizes the effective semantic information delivered per unit of time.

  • •

    We formulate a joint optimization problem that coordinates token selection, uplink transmit power, and bandwidth allocation under strict latency and energy constraints. To tackle the resulting mixed-integer nonconvex program, we develop an efficient alternating optimization algorithm.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews the background and related work. Section III presents the workflow and delay–energy analysis of ST-SFLora. Section IV presents the client selection and token selection strategies. Section V presents the new metric STE and formulates the optimization problem, and Section VI provides its solution. Section VII reports the performance evaluation. Section VIII concludes the paper.

II Related Works

FL enables collaborative model training without sharing raw data by aggregating client-side updates on a central server [8, 7]. Although effective for privacy preservation, FL becomes challenging to apply to large Transformer-based models because local fine-tuning demands substantial computation and memory on heterogeneous mobile devices. SL [10] addresses device constraints through sequential collaborative training: each client computes the early layers of a shared model, uploads the resulting activations, and receives gradients from the server before the next client proceeds. SFL [11] combines the model-partitioning idea of SL with the aggregation mechanism of FL, enabling clients to execute the early layers in parallel and upload activations, while the server completes the remaining forward–backward computation and aggregates updates across clients. The workflows of these representative paradigms are summarized in Fig. 2.

Recent works have explored adaptive and resource-aware variants of SFL. HSFL [18] integrates the parallel update mechanism of FL with the model-splitting structure of SL and incorporates a MAB-based user selection strategy to improve accuracy under heterogeneous UAV networks. CPSL [19] proposes a parallel-then-sequential split learning scheme that jointly optimizes cut-layer selection, device clustering, and spectrum allocation to reduce training latency in wireless networks. In vehicular edge intelligence, ASFV [20] dynamically selects cut layers based on mobility and resource availability. SFL has also been extended to large models: SplitLoRA [5] integrates LoRA fine-tuning into SFL to reduce trainable parameters, while SplitFrozen [21] freezes most client-side layers and also keeps part of the server-side backbone frozen, while only updating lightweight auxiliary modules to accommodate device heterogeneity and accelerate LLM fine-tuning.

Communication-efficient training has been widely studied in distributed learning. Bit-level compression techniques such as gradient quantization [14, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26] and sparsification [15, 27] reduce gradient communication in FL. In SL and SFL, activation compression [13, 28, 29] has received increasing attention, as transmitting intermediate features often dominates uplink costs. As wireless networks evolve toward 6G, task-oriented semantic communication [16, 30] promotes transmitting only task-relevant information. However, existing SL/SFL frameworks still rely on bit-level compression and have not exploited the semantic structure of Transformer activations—whose representation is naturally tokenized and semantically structured—for selective activation transmission or communication optimization under mobility-induced channel variation.

Existing SL and SFL frameworks struggle to support efficient fine-tuning of large Transformer models on mobile edge devices, due to heavy communication overhead and the need for bidirectional exchanges of large activations. Prior compression methods operate at the bit level and ignore the token-level semantic structure of Transformer activations. In mobile scenarios, mobility-induced channel variations further worsen the communication bottleneck, but are rarely considered together with wireless resource constraints and semantic relevance. These limitations motivate the proposed ST-SFLora framework, which (i) reduces client–server interactions, (ii) leverages token-level semantics to guide activation transmission, and (iii) jointly optimizes token selection and wireless communication resources.

III ST-SFLora: Overview and Delay-Energy Analysis

In this section, we first present the system overview of ST-SFLora, and then describe its training workflow along with the corresponding delay-energy analysis.

III-A Architecture Overview

The proposed ST-SFLora framework is tailored for collaborative fine-tuning over MEC networks. The system comprises an edge server and a set of edge devices ℳ={1,2,…,M}\mathcal{M}=\{1,2,\dots,M\}. Each device m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M} stores a private dataset 𝒟m={(𝒳m,𝒴m)}\mathcal{D}_{m}=\{(\mathcal{X}_{m},\mathcal{Y}_{m})\} with DmD_{m} labeled samples. Training proceeds over communication rounds t∈{1,2,…,T}t\in\{1,2,\dots,T\}. Due to limited wireless bandwidth and time-varying channels, only a subset of clients 𝒰t⊆ℳ\mathcal{U}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{M} participates in round tt. The global model is partitioned at cut layer ee: shallow layers run on the device, while the remaining layers are hosted on the edge server.

III-B Workflow and Delay-Energy Analysis

The overall workflow of the proposed ST-SFLora framework consists of six phases, as illustrated in Fig. 3. The training procedure is summarized in Alg. 1. The detailed process of each phase is described as follows.

III-B1 Client Selection and Model Broadcasting

At the beginning of each global round tt, the edge server collects the channel state information (CSI) and status of devices within its communication range and performs mobility-aware client selection. The resulting active client set is denoted by 𝒰t⊆ℳ\mathcal{U}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{M}, and the server broadcasts the pre-trained client-side model parameters 𝝎c\boldsymbol{\omega}^{c} to all clients m∈𝒰tm\in\mathcal{U}_{t}.

The control signaling for client selection is negligible compared with the transmission of activation tokens and is therefore ignored. The downlink broadcasting rate is RD​L=Wtot​log2⁡(1+ps​hminN0​Wtot)R^{DL}=W_{\mathrm{tot}}\log_{2}\!\left(1+\frac{p_{s}h_{\min}}{N_{0}W_{\mathrm{tot}}}\right), where hmin=minm∈ℳ⁡hmh_{\min}=\min_{m\in\mathcal{M}}h_{m} represents the weakest channel gain among all participating clients, psp_{s} is the downlink power of sever, WtotW_{\mathrm{tot}} is the overall bandwidth. Accordingly, the broadcasting delay for a model of size s0s_{0} bits can be expressed as

TD​L=s0RD​L.T^{DL}=\frac{s_{0}}{R^{DL}}. (1)

III-B2 Client-Side Feature Extraction and Tokenization

Each participating client m∈𝒰tm\in\mathcal{U}_{t} performs forward propagation to extract local feature representations using the client-side model. Specifically, given a local mini-batch ℬm={(xb,yb)}b=1B\mathcal{B}_{m}=\{(x_{b},y_{b})\}_{b=1}^{B} sampled from the private dataset 𝒟m\mathcal{D}_{m}, the client computes the intermediate activations as: Am=ℓ⁡(𝝎c,ℬm)A_{m}=\ell\!\big(\boldsymbol{\omega}^{c},\,\mathcal{B}_{m}\big), where ℓ⁡(⋅)\ell(\cdot) denotes the local forward function that maps the input mini-batch ℬm\mathcal{B}_{m} to a sequence of tokens Am∈ℝB×(N+1)×DA_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times(N+1)\times D}.2

Since all clients execute this phase in parallel, we analyze the local computation delay for an individual client. Let γcF=∑j=1eρj\gamma^{F}_{c}=\sum_{j=1}^{e}\rho_{j} represent the total computational complexity (in FLOPs) of the client-side model per sample, where ρj\rho_{j} denotes the workload of the jj-th layer and ee is the total number of client-side layers. Consequently, the computation latency for client mm to process a mini-batch of size BB is formulated as:

TmF=B​γcFfm​Cm​DmU,T^{F}_{m}=\frac{B\,\gamma^{F}_{c}}{f_{m}\,C_{m}\,D^{U}_{m}}, (2)

where fmf_{m} is the GPU clock frequency of client mm, CmC_{m} is the number of computing cores, and DmUD^{U}_{m} represents the floating-point operations per cycle per core.

22footnotetext: Given an image I∈ℝH×W×CI\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C}, the patch-embedding layer first splits II into NN non-overlapping patches and flattens them into Ip∈ℝN×(P2​C)I_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times(P^{2}C)}, where (H,W)(H,W) represents the height and width of the input image, (P,P)(P,P) is the resolution of each image patch, CC denotes the number of channels, and N=H​W/P2N=HW/P^{2} is the number of image tokens. The flattened patches IpI_{p} are then mapped to A0=[a1,a2,…,aN]∈ℝN×DA^{0}=[a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{N}]\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} using a trainable linear projection. Finally, a learnable [CLS] token a0a_{0} is prepended to form [a0,a1,…,aN]∈ℝ(N+1)×D[a_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}]\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times D}, which serves as the input to the Transformer layers.

III-B3 Token Importance Uploading

For each sample in the mini-batch, the final client-side Transformer block outputs a set of tokens accompanied by attention scores that indicate their relative semantic importance. To characterize the global attention distribution, the client sorts the tokens of each sample in descending order of importance and sums the attention values rank-wise across the batch. This operation yields a batch-level token importance vector 𝜶¯m=[α¯m,1,α¯m,2,…,α¯m,N]\bar{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{m}=[\bar{\alpha}_{m,1},\bar{\alpha}_{m,2},\ldots,\bar{\alpha}_{m,N}]. Subsequently, each client transmits this batch-level token importance vector to the server. Since these vectors consist of lightweight scalar quantities, the transmission latency and energy consumption of this phase are considered negligible and are ignored in the subsequent analysis.

III-B4 Optimization

Utilizing the received CSI and the batch-level token importance vectors, the server performs joint optimization of the token budget 𝑲\boldsymbol{K}, uplink transmit power 𝒑\boldsymbol{p}, and bandwidth allocation 𝑾\boldsymbol{W}. Upon solving the optimization problem, the server distributes the optimal parameters {𝑲∗,𝒑∗,𝑾∗}\{\boldsymbol{K}^{*},\boldsymbol{p}^{*},\boldsymbol{W}^{*}\} back to the selected clients. Similar to the previous phase, the computational time for this optimization and the downlink latency for broadcasting these control parameters are omitted from the delay-energy analysis, as they are minimal compared to the training and activation transmission costs.

III-B5 Selected Token Uploading

Upon receiving the optimized parameters, each selected client applies the semantic-aware token selection strategy based on the assigned token budget Km∗K_{m}^{*} and communication parameters (Wm∗,pm∗)(W_{m}^{*},p_{m}^{*}). Only the refined activations Amref∈ℝB×(Km∗+2)×DA_{m}^{\mathrm{ref}}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times(K_{m}^{*}+2)\times D} are transmitted to the server over the allocated bandwidth. This selective transmission effectively reduces communication overhead while preserving sufficient semantic information for server-side fine-tuning.

To upload the selected tokens, the total bandwidth WtotW_{\mathrm{tot}} is partitioned among the active clients. Let WmW_{m} denote the bandwidth allocated to client mm in round tt, where ∑m∈𝒰tWm≤Wtot\sum_{m\in\mathcal{U}_{t}}W_{m}\leq W_{\mathrm{tot}}. The achievable uplink transmission rate for client mm is given by:

RmU​L=Wm​log2⁡(1+pm∗​hmN0​Wm),R_{m}^{UL}=W_{m}\log_{2}\left(1+\frac{p_{m}^{*}h_{m}}{N_{0}W_{m}}\right), (3)

where pm∗p_{m}^{*} is the optimized transmit power, hmh_{m} is the channel gain, and N0N_{0} is the background noise power spectral density. The data size of the uploaded tokens for client mm depends on the batch size BB, the number of selected tokens Km∗K_{m}^{*}, and the embedding dimension DD. It is calculated as:

Sm\displaystyle S_{m} =B×(Km∗+2)×D×q0(bits),\displaystyle=B\times(K_{m}^{*}+2)\times D\times q_{0}\quad(\mathrm{bits}), (4)

where q0q_{0} denotes the bit-width per element (e.g., q0=32q_{0}=32 for single-precision floating-point without quantization). Consequently, the uplink communication latency and energy consumption are formulated as:

TmU\displaystyle T_{m}^{\mathrm{U}} =SmRmU​L,EmU=pm∗​TmU.\displaystyle=\frac{S_{m}}{R_{m}^{UL}},\quad E_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}=p_{m}^{*}T_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}. (5)

III-B6 Server-Side LoRA-Based Fine-Tuning

Upon receiving the refined activations from 𝒰t\mathcal{U}_{t}, the server sequentially fine-tunes the LoRA adapter Δ​𝝎s\Delta\boldsymbol{\omega}^{s} while keeping the backbone frozen. For each client m∈𝒰tm\in\mathcal{U}_{t}, the uploaded AmrefA_{m}^{\mathrm{ref}} is used to compute the loss LL and update the parameters as:

Δ𝝎m,ts←Δ𝝎m−1,ts−η∇L,\Delta\boldsymbol{\omega}_{m,t}^{s}\leftarrow\Delta\boldsymbol{\omega}_{m-1,t}^{s}-\eta\,\nabla L, (6)

where Δ​𝝎0,ts=Δ​𝝎t−1s\Delta\boldsymbol{\omega}_{0,t}^{s}=\Delta\boldsymbol{\omega}_{t-1}^{s} inherits the global state from the previous round. This phase finalizes the learning for round tt. Given the server’s sufficient computational capacity, the associated latency and energy consumption are omitted from our analysis.

IV Client Selection and Token Selection

In this section, we first introduce a mobility-aware client selection scheme to ensure reliable participation within the server coverage. We then propose a semantic-aware token selection approach that combines attention-driven selection with token merging.

IV-A Mobility-aware Client Selection

Prior to the commencement of local training, the server determines which clients are eligible to participate in the current round. Due to the limited communication range of the edge server, high-mobility clients risk exiting the coverage area during the training process, leading to potential transmission failures. Consequently, not all clients can be selected in each round, and a mobility-aware selection strategy is required to ensure stable participation and reliable model updates.

We define the standing time as the duration a client remains within the server’s effective communication range. Let vmv_{m} denote the velocity of client mm, which is assumed constant during one round. Let LL represent the coverage radius of the server, and lml_{m} denote the current radial distance of client mm from the server. Thus, the remaining distance to the coverage boundary is L−lmL-l_{m}. Given the maximum latency constraint per iteration t¯\bar{t}, the effective standing time of client mm is defined as:

Tmstanding=min⁡{L−lmvm,t¯}.T_{m}^{\mathrm{standing}}=\min\!\left\{\frac{L-l_{m}}{v_{m}},\,\bar{t}\right\}. (7)

To ensure successful completion, the client’s standing time must exceed the total time required for interaction, denoted as the holding time. As illustrated in Fig. 4, holding time is calculated as:

Tmholding=Tm0+TmU,T_{m}^{\mathrm{holding}}=T_{m}^{0}+T_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}, (8)

where Tm0=TD+TmFT_{m}^{0}=T^{\mathrm{D}}+T_{m}^{\mathrm{F}} represents the sum of the downlink broadcasting delay and the local forward computation time, while TmUT_{m}^{\mathrm{U}} denotes the uplink transmission time. A binary client selection indicator θmt\theta_{m}^{t} is then defined as:

θmt={1,ifTmholding≤Tmstanding,0,otherwise,\theta_{m}^{t}=\begin{cases}1,&\mathrm{if\quad}T_{m}^{\mathrm{holding}}\leq T_{m}^{\mathrm{standing}},\\ 0,&\mathrm{otherwise},\end{cases} (9)

where θmt=1\theta_{m}^{t}=1 indicates that client mm can complete the training task within the coverage area and is selected for this round, while θmt=0\theta_{m}^{t}=0 indicates exclusion due to the risk of disconnection. Accordingly, the selected client set is given by:

𝒰t={m∈ℳ∣θmt=1}.\mathcal{U}_{t}=\{\,m\in\mathcal{M}\mid\theta_{m}^{t}=1\,\}. (10)

IV-B Semantic-aware Token Selection Strategy

In this subsection, we present a semantic-aware token selection strategy that exploits the self-attention mechanism of Transformer architectures to suppress redundant tokens while preserving task-relevant context.

IV-B1 Token Selection

In Vision Transformers, the [CLS] token serves as a global feature aggregator, attending to all patch tokens to synthesize task-discriminative representations. Consequently, the attention weights assigned by the [CLS] token serve as a reliable proxy for task relevance. Tokens with higher attention scores typically contribute more to the final prediction, whereas those with lower scores are often redundant background features.

For each client mm, let 𝐀m∈ℝB×(N+1)×D\mathbf{A}_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times(N+1)\times D} denoted the intermediate activation tensor obtained from client-side forward propagation, where BB denotes the batch size, NN the number of patch tokens, and DD the embedding dimension. The token sequence of the bb-th image is represented as 𝐀m(b)=[𝐚m,0(b),𝐚m,1(b),…,𝐚m,N(b)]\mathbf{A}_{m}^{(b)}=[\mathbf{a}_{m,0}^{(b)},\mathbf{a}_{m,1}^{(b)},\ldots,\mathbf{a}_{m,N}^{(b)}], where 𝐚m,0(b)\mathbf{a}_{m,0}^{(b)} is the [CLS] token and 𝐚m,n(b)\mathbf{a}_{m,n}^{(b)} (n=1,…,Nn=1,\ldots,N) are patch tokens. In the final client-side Transformer block, the self-attention map is computed as

𝐀𝐭𝐭m(b)=softmax⁡(𝐐m(b)​𝐊m(b)⊤D),\mathbf{Att}_{m}^{(b)}=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}_{m}^{(b)}\mathbf{K}_{m}^{(b)\top}}{\sqrt{D}}\right), (11)

where 𝐐m(b)\mathbf{Q}_{m}^{(b)} and 𝐊m(b)\mathbf{K}_{m}^{(b)} denote the query and key matrices derived from 𝐀m(b)\mathbf{A}_{m}^{(b)}. The attention score between the [CLS] token and the nn-th patch token is calculated as

αm,n(b)=exp⁡(𝐪m,0(b)⋅𝐤m,n(b))∑j=1Nexp⁡(𝐪m,0(b)⋅𝐤m,j(b)),\alpha_{m,n}^{(b)}=\frac{\exp\!\left(\mathbf{q}_{m,0}^{(b)}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{k}_{m,n}^{(b)}\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp\!\left(\mathbf{q}_{m,0}^{(b)}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{k}_{m,j}^{(b)}\right)}, (12)

where 𝐪m,0(b)\mathbf{q}_{m,0}^{(b)} and 𝐤m,n(b)\mathbf{k}_{m,n}^{(b)} denote the query and key vectors corresponding to the [CLS] token and the nn-th patch token, respectively. The score αm,n(b)\alpha_{m,n}^{(b)} quantifies the dependency of the [CLS] token on the nn-th patch token, serving as an indicator of its semantic importance. Leveraging these scores, each client identifies and retains only the top-KmK_{m} most informative tokens (excluding the [CLS] token):

𝐀msel={𝐚m,n(b)|n∈Top−Km​(αm,1(b),…,αm,N(b))}b=1B.\mathbf{A}_{m}^{\mathrm{sel}}=\big\{\,\mathbf{a}_{m,n}^{(b)}\,\big|\,n\!\in\!\mathrm{Top}\mathrm{-}K_{m}(\alpha_{m,1}^{(b)},\ldots,\alpha_{m,N}^{(b)})\big\}_{b=1}^{B}. (13)

The number of selected tokens KmK_{m} is determined adaptively through the optimization process, thereby reducing redundant tokens and communication overhead while preserving task-relevant information essential for downstream fine-tuning.

IV-B2 Token Merging

While token selection efficiently filters redundancy, simply discarding low-scoring tokens may lead to the loss of subtle contextual information. To mitigate this, token merging aggregates the discarded tokens into a summary representation. For each image sample bb on client mm, let 𝒮m(b)=Top​-​Km​(αm,1(b),…,αm,N(b))\mathcal{S}_{m}^{(b)}=\mathrm{Top}\text{-}K_{m}\!\left(\alpha_{m,1}^{(b)},\ldots,\alpha_{m,N}^{(b)}\right) and ℐm(b)={1,…,N}∖𝒮m(b)\mathcal{I}_{m}^{(b)}=\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{m}^{(b)}. The discarded tokens are aggregated into a single merged token via an attention-weighted average:

𝐚m,merge(b)=∑n∈ℐm(b)αm,n(b)​𝐚m,n(b)∑n∈ℐm(b)αm,n(b).\mathbf{a}_{m,\mathrm{merge}}^{(b)}=\frac{\sum_{n\in\mathcal{I}_{m}^{(b)}}\alpha_{m,n}^{(b)}\,\mathbf{a}_{m,n}^{(b)}}{\sum_{n\in\mathcal{I}_{m}^{(b)}}\alpha_{m,n}^{(b)}}. (14)

Finally, the refined token sequence is constructed by concatenating the [CLS] token, the selected tokens, and the merged token. The overall refined batch representation is expressed as

𝐀mref=[𝐚m,0(b),{𝐚m,n(b)}n∈𝒮m(b),𝐚m,merge(b)]b=1B,\mathbf{A}_{m}^{\mathrm{ref}}=\Big[\,\mathbf{a}_{m,0}^{(b)},\;\{\mathbf{a}_{m,n}^{(b)}\}_{n\in\mathcal{S}_{m}^{(b)}},\;\mathbf{a}_{m,\mathrm{merge}}^{(b)}\,\Big]_{b=1}^{B}, (15)

where 𝐀mref∈ℝB×(Km+2)×D\mathbf{A}_{m}^{\mathrm{ref}}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times(K_{m}+2)\times D}. By condensing the discarded tokens rather than removing them, the model preserves global context while substantially reducing the transmission load to the server.

V Problem Formulation

In this section, we begin by defining a new metric to explicitly quantify the trade-off between semantic information retention and communication latency. Building upon this metric, we then construct the joint optimization problem to determine the optimal token-level transmission and communication resource allocation.

V-A New Metric: Semantic Transmission Efficiency

For each client mm, the final Transformer block of the client-side model produces a sequence of tokens for each image sample bb in the mini-batch:

𝐀m(b)=[𝐚m,0(b),𝐚m,1(b),…,𝐚m,N(b)]∈ℝ(N+1)×D,\mathbf{A}_{m}^{(b)}=[\mathbf{a}_{m,0}^{(b)},\mathbf{a}_{m,1}^{(b)},\ldots,\mathbf{a}_{m,N}^{(b)}]\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times D}, (16)

where 𝐚m,0(b)\mathbf{a}_{m,0}^{(b)} denotes the [CLS] token and {𝐚m,n(b)}n=1N\{\mathbf{a}_{m,n}^{(b)}\}_{n=1}^{N} are patch tokens. The attention score αm,n(b)\alpha_{m,n}^{(b)} measures the task relevance of each token, as defined in (12).Sorting these scores in descending order yields

αm,1(b)≥αm,2(b)≥⋯≥αm,N(b).\alpha_{m,1}^{(b)}\geq\alpha_{m,2}^{(b)}\geq\cdots\geq\alpha_{m,N}^{(b)}. (17)

Since resource optimization is performed before each communication round, which transmits a complete mini-batch, a unified token budget KmK_{m} must be determined for the entire batch. To maximize the total semantic information retained in each round, we therefore compute a batch-level token importance:

α¯m,n=∑b=1Bαm,n(b),𝜶¯m=[α¯m,1,α¯m,2,…,α¯m,N],\bar{\alpha}_{m,n}=\sum_{b=1}^{B}\alpha_{m,n}^{(b)},\quad\bar{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{m}=[\bar{\alpha}_{m,1},\bar{\alpha}_{m,2},\ldots,\bar{\alpha}_{m,N}], (18)

where α¯m,n\bar{\alpha}_{m,n} represents the total semantic contribution of the nn-th ranked token summed across the mini-batch. The cumulative semantic information retention preserved by selecting the top-KmK_{m} tokens is then expressed as:

fm​(Km)=∑n=1Kmα¯m,n,f_{m}(K_{m})=\sum_{n=1}^{K_{m}}\bar{\alpha}_{m,n}, (19)

which quantifies the total semantic information retained after filtering. As illustrated in Fig. 5, this function fm​(Km)f_{m}(K_{m}) exhibits concavity, as formally proven in Lemma 1.

Lemma 1.

Let {αm,n(b)}n=1N\{\alpha_{m,n}^{(b)}\}_{n=1}^{N} denote the normalized attention scores of the bb-th sample for client mm, sorted such that αm,1(b)≥⋯≥αm,N(b)\alpha_{m,1}^{(b)}\geq\cdots\geq\alpha_{m,N}^{(b)}. Then, the cumulative semantic information retention function fm​(Km)f_{m}(K_{m}) defined in (19) is monotonically increasing and concave with respect to KmK_{m}.

Proof.

Since αm,n(b)≥0\alpha_{m,n}^{(b)}\geq 0 and the summed importance scores maintain the non-increasing order α¯m,1≥α¯m,2≥⋯≥α¯m,N\bar{\alpha}_{m,1}\geq\bar{\alpha}_{m,2}\geq\cdots\geq\bar{\alpha}_{m,N}, the first-order difference is fm​(Km+1)−fm​(Km)=α¯m,Km+1≥0f_{m}(K_{m}+1)-f_{m}(K_{m})=\bar{\alpha}_{m,K_{m}+1}\geq 0, implying monotonicity. Furthermore, the inequality α¯m,Km+1≤α¯m,Km\bar{\alpha}_{m,K_{m}+1}\leq\bar{\alpha}_{m,K_{m}} indicates diminishing marginal gains, thereby establishing the concavity of fm​(Km)f_{m}(K_{m}) in the discrete domain. ∎

At the system level, the total semantic information retention is derived by summing the individual contributions ∑m∈𝒰fm​(Km)\sum_{m\in\mathcal{U}}f_{m}(K_{m}). To explicitly capture the trade-off between semantic information retention and communication latency, we define the STE as:

ℰ=ΔT=∑m∈𝒰fm​(Km)maxm∈𝒰​{TmU},\mathcal{E}=\frac{\Delta}{T}=\frac{\sum_{m\in\mathcal{U}}f_{m}(K_{m})}{\underset{m\in\mathcal{U}}{\max}\{T_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}\}}, (20)

where the numerator quantifies the total semantic information retained by all participating clients, while the denominator represents the bottleneck communication latency per round, dominated by the straggler due to the synchronous aggregation requirement. As an efficiency metric, ℰ\mathcal{E} measures the rate of effective semantic information delivery. A higher value of ℰ\mathcal{E} indicates that the system achieves greater learning contribution under lower latency, thereby facilitating more efficient distributed training. As shown in Fig. 6, the STE curve exhibits a distinct peak. This validates the existence of an optimal trade-off, where the marginal information gain matches the marginal latency cost.

Remark 1.

The metric STE can be interpreted as the system-level semantic throughput. Unlike conventional throughput (measured in bits per second), STE quantifies the density of task-relevant utility delivered per unit of time. Physically, maximizing STE identifies the optimal operating point where the marginal gain of retaining additional tokens matches the marginal cost of the induced time delay from the bottleneck straggler. We use maxm∈𝒰t⁡TmU\max_{m\in\mathcal{U}_{t}}{T_{m}^{U}} since STE is a system metric and the uplink phase is bounded by the last-finishing client.

V-B Problem Formulation

Given the STE metric defined in (20), we formulate the system-level objective to jointly optimize the token selection 𝑲\boldsymbol{K}, bandwidth allocation 𝑾\boldsymbol{W}, and transmission power 𝒑\boldsymbol{p}. Our goal is to maximize the semantic transmission efficiency in each communication round. This formulation mathematically encapsulates the trade-off between semantic information retention and communication latency:

𝒫​0:\displaystyle\mathcal{P}0:\quad max𝑲,𝑾,𝒑ℰ=∑m∈𝒰fm​(Km)maxm∈𝒰​TmU\displaystyle\max_{\boldsymbol{K},\,\boldsymbol{W},\,\boldsymbol{p}}\quad\mathcal{E}=\frac{\sum_{m\in\mathcal{U}}f_{m}(K_{m})}{\underset{m\in\mathcal{U}}{\max}\,T_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}} (21a)
s.t. C1:0≤pm≤pmax,∀m∈𝒰,\displaystyle\text{C1:}\quad 0\leq p_{m}\leq p^{\max},\quad\forall m\in\mathcal{U}, (21b)
C2:∑m∈𝒰Wm≤Wtot,\displaystyle\text{C2:}\quad\sum_{m\in\mathcal{U}}W_{m}\leq W_{\mathrm{tot}}, (21c)
C3:Wm≥0,∀m∈𝒰,\displaystyle\text{C3:}\quad W_{m}\geq 0,\quad\forall m\in\mathcal{U}, (21d)
C4:Kmin≤Km≤N,Km∈ℤ,∀m∈𝒰,\displaystyle\text{C4:}\quad K^{\min}\leq K_{m}\leq N,\quad K_{m}\in\mathbb{Z},\quad\forall m\in\mathcal{U}, (21e)
C5:EmU(Km,Wm,pm)≤Emax,∀m∈𝒰,\displaystyle\text{C5:}\quad E_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(K_{m},W_{m},p_{m})\leq E^{\max},\quad\forall m\in\mathcal{U}, (21f)
C6:Tm0+TmU(Km,Wm,pm)≤Tmstanding,∀m∈𝒰.\displaystyle\text{C6:}\quad T_{m}^{0}+T_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(K_{m},W_{m},p_{m})\leq T_{m}^{\mathrm{standing}},\quad\forall m\in\mathcal{U}. (21g)

Constraint C1 sets the range for transmission power, while Constraints C2 and C3 manage the total bandwidth allocation. These variables are continuous. Constraint C4 restricts the number of selected tokens to be an integer. Finally, Constraints C5 and C6 ensure that the energy consumption and total latency do not exceed the specific limits of each client.

VI Problem Solution

Problem 𝒫​0\mathcal{P}0 in (21a) jointly optimizes the token selection vector 𝑲\boldsymbol{K}, bandwidth allocation 𝑾\boldsymbol{W}, and transmit power 𝒑\boldsymbol{p}. The objective is a fractional function with a denominator that contains a maximization operator, and the feasible set involves both continuous and integer variables. Hence, 𝒫​0\mathcal{P}0 is a mixed-integer nonlinear program that is difficult to solve directly. To eliminate the maximization operator in the denominator, we introduce an auxiliary variable

τ≜maxm∈𝒰⁡TmU​(Km,Wm,pm),\tau\triangleq\max_{m\in\mathcal{U}}T_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(K_{m},W_{m},p_{m}), (22)

which can be enforced through the set of constraints

TmU​(Km,Wm,pm)≤τ,∀m∈𝒰.T_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(K_{m},W_{m},p_{m})\leq\tau,\quad\forall m\in\mathcal{U}. (23)

Using τ\tau, problem 𝒫​0\mathcal{P}0 can be equivalently rewritten as

𝒫​0′:\displaystyle\mathcal{P}0^{\prime}:\quad max𝑲,𝑾,𝒑,τ⁡∑m∈𝒰fm​(Km)τ\displaystyle\max_{\boldsymbol{K},\,\boldsymbol{W},\,\boldsymbol{p},\,\tau}\ \frac{\sum_{m\in\mathcal{U}}f_{m}(K_{m})}{\tau} (24a)
s.t. C1–C6 in ​(21b)​–​(21g),\displaystyle\text{C1--C6 in }(\ref{q0-1})\text{--}(\ref{q0-6}),
C7:TmU(Km,Wm,pm)≤τ,∀m∈𝒰.\displaystyle\text{C7:}\ T_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(K_{m},W_{m},p_{m})\leq\tau,\ \forall m\in\mathcal{U}. (24b)

Although the maximization operator is removed, Problem 𝒫​0′\mathcal{P}0^{\prime} remains challenging due to the intricate coupling between the integer variable 𝑲\boldsymbol{K} and the continuous resource variables (𝑾,𝒑)(\boldsymbol{W},\boldsymbol{p}) in the constraints. To address this, we propose an iterative algorithm. Since fm​(Km)≥0f_{m}(K_{m})\geq 0 holds for all m∈𝒰m\in\mathcal{U}, maximizing the fractional objective is then equivalent to minimizing the worst-case latency τ\tau under the resource, energy, and standing-time constraints. Although this transformation removes the explicit maximization operator from the denominator, problem 𝒫​0′\mathcal{P}0^{\prime} remains a nonconvex mixed-integer nonlinear program due to the coupling among 𝑲\boldsymbol{K}, 𝑾\boldsymbol{W}, and 𝒑\boldsymbol{p}. To handle this difficulty, we decompose the original problem into three coupled subproblems, namely power control, bandwidth allocation, and token selection, and solve them iteratively in an alternating manner until convergence.

Remark 2.

Decomposing a highly coupled optimization problem into multiple subproblems and solving them iteratively is commonly adopted when the original function is difficult to optimize directly (see, e.g., [31, 19, 32]). The solutions can be efficiently computed but not necessarily optimal.

VI-A Power Control

When only the transmit power vector 𝒑\boldsymbol{p} is optimized while fixing the token numbers 𝑲\boldsymbol{K} and bandwidth allocation 𝑾\boldsymbol{W}, the system-level objective in 𝒫​0′\mathcal{P}0^{\prime} reduces to minimizing the worst-case uplink latency τ=maxm∈𝒰⁡TmU​(pm)\tau=\max_{m\in\mathcal{U}}T_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(p_{m}) under the energy and standing-time constraints. Since the transmit powers of different clients are mutually independent, the power control problem can be decomposed into independent subproblems for each device. For a given device m∈𝒰m\in\mathcal{U}, the power-control subproblem 𝒮​𝒰​ℬ​𝒫​1\mathcal{SUBP}1 can be expressed as

𝒮​𝒰​ℬ​𝒫​1:\displaystyle\mathcal{SUBP}1:\quad minpmTmU​(pm)\displaystyle\underset{p_{m}}{\min}\quad T_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(p_{m}) (25a)
s.t. C1,C5-C6\displaystyle\text{C1},\text{C5-C6} (25b)

where TmU​(pm)=Sm​(Km)Wm​log2⁡(1+pm​hmn0​Wm)T_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(p_{m})=\frac{S_{m}(K_{m})}{W_{m}\log_{2}\!\left(1+\frac{p_{m}h_{m}}{n_{0}W_{m}}\right)} denotes the uplink latency of device mm. For fixed (Km,Wm)(K_{m},W_{m}), TmU​(pm)T_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(p_{m}) is strictly decreasing in pmp_{m}, and minimizing τ\tau amounts to reducing all TmUT_{m}^{\mathrm{U}} as much as possible within the feasible power region. From constraint C6, the standing-time constraint of device mm can be rewritten as

TmU​(pm)≤Tmmax≜Tmstanding−Tm0,T_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(p_{m})\leq T_{m}^{\max}\triangleq T_{m}^{\mathrm{standing}}-T_{m}^{0}, (26)

which is equivalent to the following lower bound on the transmit power:

pm≥pmmin=n0​Wmhm​(2SmWm​Tmmax−1).p_{m}\geq p_{m}^{\min}=\frac{n_{0}W_{m}}{h_{m}}\!\left(2^{\frac{S_{m}}{W_{m}T_{m}^{\max}}}-1\right). (27)

This specifies the minimum transmit power required to satisfy the latency constraint of device mm.

Theorem 1.

EmU​(pm)E_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(p_{m}) is strictly increasing in pmp_{m} for pm>0p_{m}>0.

Proof.

Let ϕm≜hmn0​Wm>0\phi_{m}\triangleq\tfrac{h_{m}}{n_{0}W_{m}}>0. The uplink communication energy consumption of device mm can be rewritten as

EmU​(pm)\displaystyle\small E_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(p_{m}) =pm​SmWm​log2⁡(1+ϕm​pm)\displaystyle=\frac{p_{m}S_{m}}{W_{m}\,\log_{2}(1+\phi_{m}p_{m})}
=Sm​ln⁡2Wm⏟χ>0⋅pmln⁡(1+ϕm​pm)≜χ​G~​(pm),\displaystyle=\underbrace{\frac{S_{m}\ln 2}{W_{m}}}_{\chi>0}\cdot\frac{p_{m}}{\ln(1+\phi_{m}p_{m})}\;\triangleq\;\chi\,\tilde{G}(p_{m}), (28)

where G~​(p)=pln⁡(1+ϕm​p)\tilde{G}(p)=\dfrac{p}{\ln(1+\phi_{m}p)}. It suffices to show that G~​(p)\tilde{G}(p) is strictly increasing for p>0p>0. The derivative is

G~′​(p)=ln⁡(1+ϕm​p)−ϕm​p1+ϕm​p[ln⁡(1+ϕm​p)]2=ψ⁡(ϕm​p)[ln⁡(1+ϕm​p)]2,\small\tilde{G}^{\prime}(p)=\frac{\ln(1+\phi_{m}p)-\frac{\phi_{m}p}{1+\phi_{m}p}}{\big[\ln(1+\phi_{m}p)\big]^{2}}=\frac{\psi(\phi_{m}p)}{\big[\ln(1+\phi_{m}p)\big]^{2}}, (29)

where ψ⁡(x)=ln⁡(1+x)−x1+x\psi(x)=\ln(1+x)-\tfrac{x}{1+x} for x>0x>0. Since ψ′​(x)=x(1+x)2>0\psi^{\prime}(x)=\tfrac{x}{(1+x)^{2}}>0 and ψ⁡(0)=0\psi(0)=0, we have ψ⁡(x)>0\psi(x)>0 for x>0x>0. Thus G~′​(p)>0\tilde{G}^{\prime}(p)>0 for p>0p>0, proving that EmU​(Km,Wm,pm)=χ​G~​(pm)E_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(K_{m},W_{m},p_{m})=\chi\,\tilde{G}(p_{m}) is strictly increasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty).

This completes the proof. ∎

Since TmU​(pm)T_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(p_{m}) is strictly decreasing and EmU​(pm)E_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(p_{m}) is strictly increasing with respect to pmp_{m}, the optimal transmit power corresponds to the largest feasible value that satisfies all constraints. To characterize the upper bound induced by the energy constraint C5, define

Φm​(pm)=ln⁡(1+ϕm​pm)−κm​pm,\Phi_{m}(p_{m})=\ln(1+\phi_{m}p_{m})-\kappa_{m}p_{m}, (30)

where κm=Sm​ln⁡2Emax​Wm,ϕm=hmn0​Wm\kappa_{m}=\tfrac{S_{m}\ln 2}{E^{\max}W_{m}},\phi_{m}=\tfrac{h_{m}}{n_{0}W_{m}}. The constraint EmU​(pm)≤EmaxE_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(p_{m})\leq E^{\max} is equivalent to Φm​(pm)≥0\Phi_{m}(p_{m})\geq 0. We have

Φm′​(pm)\displaystyle\Phi_{m}^{\prime}(p_{m}) =ϕm1+ϕm​pm−κm,\displaystyle=\frac{\phi_{m}}{1+\phi_{m}p_{m}}-\kappa_{m},\qquad (31)
Φm′′​(pm)\displaystyle\Phi_{m}^{\prime\prime}(p_{m}) =−ϕm2(1+ϕm​pm)2<0,\displaystyle=-\frac{\phi_{m}^{2}}{(1+\phi_{m}p_{m})^{2}}<0, (32)

which implies that Φm​(pm)\Phi_{m}(p_{m}) is strictly concave on pm≥0p_{m}\geq 0 with Φm​(0)=0\Phi_{m}(0)=0 and limpm→∞Φm​(pm)=−∞\lim_{p_{m}\to\infty}\Phi_{m}(p_{m})=-\infty. Therefore, as illustrated in Fig. 7, the feasibility structure of the energy constraint can be characterized as follows:

  • •

    If pmax​SmWm​log2⁡(1+ϕm​pmax)≤Emax\frac{p^{\max}S_{m}}{W_{m}\log_{2}\!\left(1+\phi_{m}p^{\max}\right)}\leq E^{\max}, then Φm​(pmax)≥0\Phi_{m}(p^{\max})\geq 0, indicating that the energy constraint is inactive over [0,pmax][0,p^{\max}] and all powers up to the peak limit are feasible.

  • •

    If κm≥ϕm\kappa_{m}\geq\phi_{m}, then Φm′​(pm)≤0\Phi_{m}^{\prime}(p_{m})\leq 0 for all pm≥0p_{m}\geq 0, which implies Φm​(pm)≤Φm​(0)=0\Phi_{m}(p_{m})\leq\Phi_{m}(0)=0 for any pm>0p_{m}>0. Hence, no strictly positive transmit power can satisfy EmU≤EmaxE_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}\!\leq E^{\max}.

    If 0<κm<ϕm0<\kappa_{m}<\phi_{m} and Φm​(pmax)<0\Phi_{m}(p^{\max})<0, then the strict concavity of Φm\Phi_{m} guarantees the existence of a unique root p¯m∈(0,pmax)\bar{p}_{m}\in(0,p^{\max}) satisfying Φm​(p¯m)=0\Phi_{m}(\bar{p}_{m})=0. Consequently, the feasible power region induced by the energy constraint is the interval [0,p¯m][0,\,\bar{p}_{m}].

Combining the peak-power limit, the latency-induced lower bound, and the energy constraint, the optimal transmit power admits the compact form

pm⋆={pmax,EmU​(pmax)≤Emax​and​pmax≥pmmin,min⁡{pmax,p¯m},0<κm<ϕm​and​pmmin≤p¯m,infeasible,otherwise.p_{m}^{\star}=\begin{cases}p^{\max},&E_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(p^{\max})\leq E^{\max}\ \text{and}\ p^{\max}\geq p_{m}^{\min},\\[4.0pt] \min\{p^{\max},\,\bar{p}_{m}\},&0<\kappa_{m}<\phi_{m}\ \text{and}\ p_{m}^{\min}\leq\bar{p}_{m},\\[4.0pt] \text{infeasible},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (33)

For the practical case 0<κm<ϕm0<\kappa_{m}<\phi_{m} and EmU​(pmax)>EmaxE_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(p^{\max})>E^{\max}, the unique root p¯m\bar{p}_{m} of Φm​(pm)=0\Phi_{m}(p_{m})=0 can be efficiently found using the bisection method over the interval [0,pmax][0,p^{\max}], owing to the strict concavity of Φm​(pm)\Phi_{m}(p_{m}). The details are shown in Alg. 2.

VI-B Bandwidth Allocation

Given the transmission power 𝒑\boldsymbol{p} and token selection 𝑲\boldsymbol{K}, the bandwidth allocation subproblem is formulated as:

min𝑾,τ\displaystyle\min_{\boldsymbol{W},\tau}\quad τ\displaystyle\tau
s.t.\displaystyle\mathrm{s.t.}\quad C​2,C​3,C​5,C​6,C​7.\displaystyle C2,\,C3,\,C5,\,C6,\,C7.

The constraints C2–C7 imposes an effective latency upper bound on each user mm: TmU​(Wm)≤T¯m​(τ)T_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(W_{m})\leq\bar{T}_{m}(\tau), where T¯m​(τ)=min⁡{τ,Emax/pm,Tmstanding−Tm0}\bar{T}_{m}(\tau)=\min\{\tau,\;E^{\max}/p_{m},\;T_{m}^{\mathrm{standing}}-T_{m}^{0}\}. To satisfy this deadline, the allocated bandwidth must support a minimum transmission rate RmU​L​(Wm)≥Rmmin​(τ)R_{m}^{\mathrm{U}L}(W_{m})\geq R_{m}^{\min}(\tau), with

Rmmin​(τ)=max⁡{Sm​(Km)τ,pm​Sm​(Km)Emax,Sm​(Km)Tmstanding−Tm0}.\small R_{m}^{\min}(\tau)=\max\left\{\frac{S_{m}(K_{m})}{\tau},\;\frac{p_{m}S_{m}(K_{m})}{E^{\max}},\;\frac{S_{m}(K_{m})}{T_{m}^{\mathrm{standing}}-T_{m}^{0}}\right\}. (34)

Since the uplink rate function RmU​L​(Wm)R_{m}^{\mathrm{U}L}(W_{m}) is strictly increasing and concave with respect to WmW_{m}, it admits a unique inverse ψm​(⋅)\psi_{m}(\cdot). Consequently, the rate requirement translates to a bandwidth lower bound:

Wm≥Wmmin​(τ)≜ψm​(Rmmin​(τ)).W_{m}\geq W_{m}^{\min}(\tau)\triangleq\psi_{m}\big(R_{m}^{\min}(\tau)\big). (35)

Let Φ⁡(τ)=∑mWmmin​(τ)\Phi(\tau)=\sum_{m}W_{m}^{\min}(\tau) denote the total bandwidth required to achieve a system latency of τ\tau. Analyzing (34), as τ\tau decreases, the term Sm​(Km)/τS_{m}(K_{m})/\tau grows, forcing Rmmin​(τ)R_{m}^{\min}(\tau) and consequently Φ⁡(τ)\Phi(\tau) to increase. Specifically, Φ⁡(τ)\Phi(\tau) is continuous and strictly decreasing with respect to τ\tau in the region where τ\tau is the active bottleneck (i.e., when Sm/τS_{m}/\tau determines the maximum in (34)).

For the problem to be feasible, there must exist a τ\tau such that Φ⁡(τ)≤Wtot\Phi(\tau)\leq W_{\text{tot}}. The optimal latency τ⋆\tau^{\star} is the minimum value satisfying this budget constraint. Due to the monotonicity of Φ⁡(τ)\Phi(\tau), τ⋆\tau^{\star} corresponds to the unique root of the equation:

Φ⁡(τ⋆)=Wtot.\Phi(\tau^{\star})=W_{\mathrm{tot}}. (36)

Once τ⋆\tau^{\star} is determined, the optimal bandwidth allocation is uniquely given by Wm⋆=Wmmin​(τ⋆)W_{m}^{\star}=W_{m}^{\min}(\tau^{\star}). Solving for (𝑾⋆,τ⋆)(\boldsymbol{W}^{\star},\tau^{\star}) thus reduces to a one-dimensional search for the root of Φ⁡(τ)=Wtot\Phi(\tau)=W_{\mathrm{tot}}. Since the inverse Shannon capacity ψm​(⋅)\psi_{m}(\cdot) lacks a closed-form expression in terms of elementary functions, we calculate Wmmin​(τ)W_{m}^{\min}(\tau) numerically. The overall procedure employs a nested bisection method: the outer loop searches for τ⋆\tau^{\star}, while the inner loop inverts the rate function, as detailed in Algorithm 3.

VI-C Token Selection

Given the bandwidth allocation 𝑾\boldsymbol{W}, transmit power 𝒑\boldsymbol{p}, and latency bound τ\tau, the token-selection subproblem of 𝒫​0′\mathcal{P}0^{\prime} becomes

𝒮​𝒰​ℬ​𝒫​3:\displaystyle\mathcal{SUBP}3:\quad max⁡∑m∈𝒰𝑲⁡fm​(Km)\displaystyle\max_{\boldsymbol{K}}\ \sum_{m\in\mathcal{U}}f_{m}(K_{m})
s.t.C4−C7.\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad\text{C4}-\text{C7}.

The payload size grows linearly with the number of selected tokens, as Sm​(Km)=B⁡(Km+2)​D​q0S_{m}(K_{m})=B\,(K_{m}+2)\,D\,q_{0}. Since (Wm,pm)(W_{m},p_{m}) are fixed in this subproblem, the uplink rate RmUL=Wm​log2⁡(1+pm​hmn0​Wm)R_{m}^{\mathrm{UL}}=W_{m}\log_{2}\!\left(1+\frac{p_{m}h_{m}}{n_{0}W_{m}}\right) is a constant, and the uplink latency and energy consumption reduce to TmU=βm​(Km+2)RmUL,EmU​(Km)=pm​TmU​(Km)T_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}=\frac{\beta_{m}(K_{m}+2)}{R_{m}^{\mathrm{UL}}},E_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(K_{m})=p_{m}\,T_{m}^{\mathrm{U}}(K_{m}),where βm=B​D​q0\beta_{m}=BDq_{0} denotes the number of transmitted bits per token. Substituting these expressions into the constraints yields the following linear upper bounds on KmK_{m}:

Km≤Emax​RmULpm​βm−2,\displaystyle K_{m}\leq\frac{E^{\max}R_{m}^{\mathrm{UL}}}{p_{m}\beta_{m}}-2, (38)
Km≤(Tmstanding−T0)​RmULβm−2,\displaystyle K_{m}\leq\frac{(T_{m}^{\mathrm{standing}}-T_{0})R_{m}^{\mathrm{UL}}}{\beta_{m}}-2, (39)
Km≤τ​RmULβm−2.\displaystyle K_{m}\leq\frac{\tau R_{m}^{\mathrm{UL}}}{\beta_{m}}-2. (40)

Hence, the maximum feasible token number for client mm is

Kmmax\displaystyle K_{m}^{\max} =⌊min{N,Emax​RmULpm​βm−2,\displaystyle=\left\lfloor\min\!\left\{N,\ \frac{E^{\max}R_{m}^{\mathrm{UL}}}{p_{m}\beta_{m}}-2,\right.\right. (41)
(Tmstanding−Tm0)​RmULβm−2,τ​RmULβm−2}⌋.\displaystyle\left.\left.\frac{(T_{m}^{\mathrm{standing}}-T_{m}^{0})R_{m}^{\mathrm{UL}}}{\beta_{m}}-2,\ \frac{\tau R_{m}^{\mathrm{UL}}}{\beta_{m}}-2\right\}\right\rfloor.

If Kmmax<KminK_{m}^{\max}<K^{\min}, client mm is infeasible under the current (Wm,pm,τ)(W_{m},p_{m},\tau). Otherwise, the per-client decision reduces to the one-dimensional discrete maximization

Km⋆=arg⁡maxKmin≤Km≤Kmmax​fm​(Km).K_{m}^{\star}=\arg\max_{K^{\min}\leq K_{m}\leq K_{m}^{\max}}f_{m}(K_{m}). (42)

Since fm​(Km)f_{m}(K_{m}) is monotonically increasing in KmK_{m}, the objective is maximized by choosing the largest feasible token budget. Hence, the optimal solution to this subproblem is achieved at

Km⋆=Kmmax.K_{m}^{\star}=K_{m}^{\max}. (43)

Accordingly, each client selects the maximum number of informative tokens permitted by its latency and energy constraints.

VI-D Iterative Joint Optimization and Complexity

The original problem is decomposed into three subproblems and solved alternately, as shown in Alg. 4. In 𝒮​𝒰​ℬ​𝒫​1\mathcal{SUBP}1, each user computes its optimal transmit power via a one-dimensional bisection search, yielding a per-iteration complexity of 𝒪⁡(U​log⁡(1/εp))\mathcal{O}\!\left(U\log(1/\varepsilon_{p})\right). In 𝒮​𝒰​ℬ​𝒫​2\mathcal{SUBP}2, τ⋆\tau^{\star} is obtained by an outer bisection search, and for each candidate τ\tau the minimum required bandwidth Wmmin​(τ)W_{m}^{\min}(\tau) is computed via an inner bisection to invert RmUL​(Wm)R_{m}^{\mathrm{UL}}(W_{m}). This results in 𝒪⁡(U​log⁡(1/εW)​log⁡(1/ετ))\mathcal{O}\!\left(U\log(1/\varepsilon_{W})\log(1/\varepsilon_{\tau})\right) complexity, where ετ\varepsilon_{\tau} and εW\varepsilon_{W} are the tolerances of the outer and inner bisection loops, respectively. In 𝒮​𝒰​ℬ​𝒫​3\mathcal{SUBP}3, each user obtains the token number by evaluating the maximum feasible KmK_{m}, which incurs 𝒪⁡(U)\mathcal{O}(U) complexity. Therefore, the the total complexity is 𝒪⁡(Iiter​[U​log⁡(1/εp)+U​log⁡(1/εW)​log⁡(1/ετ)])\mathcal{O}\!\left(I_{\mathrm{iter}}\!\left[U\log(1/\varepsilon_{p})+U\log(1/\varepsilon_{W})\log(1/\varepsilon_{\tau})\right]\right), where IiterI_{\mathrm{iter}} is the number of outer iterations required for convergence.

VII Performance Evaluation

VII-A Experimental Setting

We consider a distributed wireless edge network consisting of one central server and 100100 mobile clients. To simulate dynamic device availability, the number of participating clients in each round is modeled by a Poisson distribution. These active clients are then considered for the joint optimization and training process. The clients are uniformly distributed within a coverage area with a radius of 55 to 500500m, communicating with the server via wireless uplink channels. The maximum transmit power for each client is set to 0.20.2 W, and the total system uplink bandwidth is 5050 MHz. The maximum GPU frequencies for the devices are selected from the intervals [1.0,1.5][1.0,1.5] GHz. The channel gain accounts for large-scale fading following a path-loss model with an exponent of 2.52.5. The noise power spectral density is set to −174-174 dBm/Hz. We assume that the mobile devices are equipped with GPUs, such as the Apple A15, which features 4 to 6 cores. Accordingly, the number of GPU cores on the device side, denoted as CnC_{n}, is selected from the range [4,6][4,6]. The computational capability is normalized such that the FLOPs per cycle per core is set to Dn=1D_{n}=1 for all clients.

We evaluate the proposed ST-SFLora framework on distributed image classification tasks employing Vision Transformer (ViT) backbones. All models are initialized with pretrained weights obtained from the timm library. Unless stated otherwise, the default hyperparameters are set as follows: learning rate 0.010.01, batch size 6464, and LoRA rank 1616. Experiments are conducted on three benchmarks covering both generic and fine-grained classification tasks: ImageNet100 [33], a widely-used subset of ILSVRC-2012 containing 100 classes, serving as a standard benchmark for generic object recognition; Oxford Flowers-102 [34], a fine-grained dataset consisting of 102 flower categories, characterized by large scale, pose, and light variations within classes; and CUB-200-2011 [35], a challenging fine-grained dataset comprising 200 bird species, which requires capturing subtle discriminative features to distinguish between visually similar sub-categories. We consider both IID and non-IID data partition settings. For the non-IID scenarios, the local class distributions are generated using a Dirichlet distribution with a concentration parameter α=0.5\alpha=0.5 to simulate data heterogeneity.

VII-B Performance under Different Distributed Architectures

Table I compares six representative distributed fine-tuning architectures. LocalLoRA performs LoRA-based fine-tuning locally without communication. FedLoRA follows the standard FL pipeline in which clients fine-tune LoRA modules locally and upload them for aggregation. SplitLoRA adopts the SL paradigm, where devices sequentially collaborate with the server to train a partitioned model with LoRA modules on both sides. SFLora extends LoRA into the SFL architecture, enabling parallel client participation while retaining trainable modules on both sides. ST-SFLora-Full is our proposed SFL variant that freezes all client-side parameters without communication token selection. ST-SFLora further incorporates the proposed semantic token selection mechanism to reduce uplink traffic.

LocalLoRA and FedLoRA exhibit the lowest accuracy, particularly under non-IID settings. LocalLoRA suffers from limited data diversity and insufficient data volume. In contrast, FedLoRA aggregates only the LoRA updates, whose parameter space is substantially smaller than the full model. Under heterogeneous data, these low-rank updates often point in inconsistent task-adaptive directions, leading to mutual cancellation during FedAvg aggregation. Consequently, both methods remain highly sensitive to client drift and show pronounced performance degradation under non-IID distributions.

SplitLoRA often achieves the strongest performance, and data heterogeneity has only a marginal impact on the SL framework. SFLora attains accuracy close to SplitLoRA, with differences typically within around 2%2\%. ST-SFLora-Full achieves accuracy comparable to SplitLoRA across datasets; on CUB-200-2011 with ViT-Large, it attains 87.75%, nearly matching the 87.96% of SplitLoRA. ST-SFLora (top-KK), which transmits only semantically important tokens, incurs moderate accuracy reductions but consistently outperforms all FL-based baselines, even under aggressive compression.

Table II further shows that split-based designs substantially reduce client-side resource usage when adapting ViT-B/16. The GPU memory requirement decreases from 9.0 GB (LocalLoRA/FedLoRA) to 2.3 GB (SplitLoRA/SFLora), and further to 1.4 GB with ST-SFLora. In addition, LocalLoRA and FedLoRA require broadcasting the entire model at the beginning of training, exceeding 335 MB of parameters, whereas all split-based variants eliminate this overhead entirely. Their communication cost is dominated by activation transmission, which reduces from 3​N16\tfrac{3N}{16} MB to 3​K16\tfrac{3K}{16} MB under top-KK token selection. Here, 316\tfrac{3}{16} MB corresponds to the activation footprint of a single token for one batch, computed as 316=B⋅D⋅q010242=64×768×3210242​MB.\frac{3}{16}=\frac{B\cdot D\cdot q_{0}}{1024^{2}}=\frac{64\times 768\times 32}{1024^{2}}~\text{MB}. These results indicate that ST-SFLora incurs the lowest computational and communication overheads among all compared methods. While this aggressive resource reduction leads to a slight decrease in accuracy, the performance degradation remains within a tolerable range, thereby ensuring the feasibility of fine-tuning on strictly constrained mobile devices.

VII-C Impact of Resource Allocation Optimization

The impact of the proposed joint resource allocation strategy is evaluated in Fig. 8. The optimization framework integrates power control, bandwidth allocation, and token selection, and the results demonstrate their synergistic contribution to maximizing the system’s STE. Fig. 8 illustrates the convergence of the iterative joint optimization algorithm under different energy budgets EmaxE_{\max}. In all cases, the objective value (STE) rises rapidly within the first few iterations and stabilizes within fewer than five outer loops. A larger EmaxE_{\max} yields a higher converged STE, as increased energy availability relaxes transmission constraints, enabling higher transmit power, wider bandwidth utilization, or a larger token budget. These results verify the computational efficiency and stability of the proposed optimization procedure.

Fig. 8 compares the performance of the full joint optimization against three ablated variants. Removing power control yields a moderate performance drop, indicating that adapting transmit power to channel heterogeneity is beneficial. The absence of bandwidth allocation causes a larger degradation, as fixed bandwidth division limits the achievable uplink rates. The most significant drop occurs when token selection is disabled. This result highlights that transmitting all tokens induces excessive latency overheads that outweigh the marginal semantic gain, thereby drastically reducing the transmission efficiency. The full configuration consistently achieves the highest STE across all energy budgets, demonstrating that all three components are essential for system performance.

Fig. 8 presents the average number of selected tokens under varying bandwidth WtotW_{\mathrm{tot}} and energy budgets EmaxE_{\max}. Both resources are positively correlated with the token count: increasing either dimension allows the system to preserve more semantic information. The observed surface trend indicates that energy and bandwidth act as coupled bottlenecks: limiting either resource restricts the allowable token budget, and the algorithm adaptively reduces token usage when resources become scarce. This observation highlights the complementary roles of physical-layer and semantic-layer resource management.

VII-D Effectiveness of Token Selection Strategy

The effectiveness of the proposed token selection strategy is validated through both visualization and quantitative evaluations, as shown in Figs. 9 and 10. Fig. 9 presents representative examples of the selected tokens under varying budgets KK. As KK decreases from 160160 to 6464, the model retains progressively fewer tokens. The masked regions (shown in black) primarily correspond to background clutter, while the preserved tokens concentrate on regions containing class-discriminative attributes, such as object contours, textures, and salient color patterns. This trend is consistent across bird, flower, and generic object categories, indicating that the proposed metric effectively prioritizes semantically informative patches and suppresses visual redundancy.

Fig. 10 reports the test accuracy for different token budgets (K∈{64,96,128,160}K\in\{64,96,128,160\}) compared to the full-token baseline across three datasets. Several key observations can be made. First, increasing the token budget generally improves the final accuracy. Across ImageNet100, Flowers-102, and CUB-200-2011, the performance gap between K=64K=64 and K=160K=160 is noticeable, particularly in the fine-grained classification tasks. A larger token budget preserves more spatial detail, leading to higher final accuracy. Second, for K≥128K\geq 128, the accuracy curves closely approximate the all-token baseline, suggesting that a moderate token budget is sufficient to encapsulate task-relevant semantics. In ImageNet100 and Flowers-102, K=160K=160 achieves performance nearly identical to the full-token model throughout the training process. In the challenging CUB dataset, although the all-token input remains slightly superior, K=160K=160 and K=128K=128 still achieve competitive accuracy with significantly reduced communication overhead. Third, ST-SFLora exhibits accuracy fluctuations reflecting its constraint-aware nature. To handle time-varying channels, the algorithm proactively downscales the token budget during deep fading. This mechanism trades marginal short-term accuracy for ensured system feasibility under strict resource constraints, demonstrating a robustness trade-off that static baselines lack.

VIII Conclusion

In this paper, we proposed ST-SFLora, a semantic token-based Split Federated LoRA fine-tuning framework designed to enable efficient computation and communication of large-scale Transformer-based vision models on resource-constrained mobile edge devices. We defined a Semantic Transmission Efficiency (STE) metric to quantify the system trade-off between semantic information retention and communication costs. To further enhance system efficiency, we formulated a joint optimization problem that coordinates transmit power, bandwidth allocation, and token selection to maximize the system STE. Extensive experiments on various datasets and backbones demonstrate that ST-SFLora achieves the lowest client-side resource consumption among state-of-the-art baselines.

Future work could explore more effective, learnable token selection strategies to further refine the efficiency trade-off. Additionally, generalizing the framework to other domains such as Natural Language Processing (NLP) would broaden the scope of efficient fine-tuning for foundation models.
